In general, integrated space conditioning TES systems consume more annual energy, despite reducing peak energy requirements, due to higher recharge energy demands, striking the need for designs which improve overall system round-trip efficiency. That being said, there is no standardized method for designing an integrated heat pump thermal energy storage (HP- TES) system, as numerous system architectures and design considerations exist [13], [14]. Such different system architectures can yield varying control strategies, TES considerations (materials and designs), and operational approaches [15], [16]. Additionally, throughout the literature, HP-TES systems are often modeled with simplified assumptions at specific design conditions and then extrapolated annually, which may lead to optimistic scenarios [17]. Furthermore, the US has diverse climate zones, varying heating and cooling demand profiles, and peak hours; thus, there is no single HP-TES system design applicable to all locations [18]. Literature Survey: Available HP-TES Technologies and Controls Thermal Energy Storage Technologies Thermal energy storage systems can be categorized into three types: sensible, latent, and thermochemical (Table 1). In sensible TES systems, the main modes of storage rely on the material's specific heat capacity, where the driving force for heat transfer is the material's thermal conductivity and the temperature difference of the TES system medium [19]. Nonetheless, the literature indicates that sensible TES requires a large volume of material (e.g., water), which can lead to stratification within TES tanks [15], [20], [24]. One study used water temperature variation in a heat pump water heater (HPWH), with the bottom side serving as a heat source and the top side as a heat sink, thereby further increasing the temperature variation within a sensible storage tank [25]. Given the substantial volume of sensible TES requirements and the lower specific heat capacity, a possible alternative is a latent TES system. In these systems, energy is stored through the solid-liquid and/or liquid-vapor phase transition of a material.
